import polars as pl

#| tags: [noclear]
food = (
    pl.read_csv(ub + "data/wweia_food.csv", ignore_errors=True)
    .select(
        c.id, c.day_of_week, c.time, c.meal_name, c.food_source,
        c.at_home, c.grams, c.kcal, c.protein, c.carbs, c.sugar, c.fat

### Questions

The same table as last week: 173,174 food items reported by 11,925 people, one row per
item. `id` is the person, `time` is the hour of the day (0 to 23), `meal_name` is the
meal, `food_source` is where the food came from, `at_home` is `"Yes"` or `"No"`,
`grams` is the mass of the item, and `kcal` is its calories.

Last week was about what to draw. This week is about how it is drawn: scales, facets,
labels, and themes.

Unless a question says otherwise, just print the result of each block; do not save it
to a variable.

1. Start with a warm-up. Group by `id` and compute each person's total `grams` and
total `kcal` for the day.

```{python}
(
    food
    .group_by(c.id)
    .agg(
        grams = c.grams.sum(),
        kcal = c.kcal.sum()
    )
)
```

2. Take the code from the previous question and draw a scatter plot of `kcal` against
`grams` with `alpha=0.05`.

```{python}
(
    food
    .group_by(c.id)
    .agg(
        grams = c.grams.sum(),
        kcal = c.kcal.sum()
    )
    .ggplot(aes(c.grams, c.kcal))
    .geom_point(alpha=0.05)
)
```

3. Now one row per person per meal. Filter to the four main meals with
`c.meal_name.is_in(["Breakfast", "Lunch", "Dinner", "Snack"])`, group by `id` and
`meal_name`, and compute the total `grams` and `kcal`. Draw a scatter plot of `kcal`
against `grams`, colored by `meal_name`, with `alpha=0.2`.

```{python}
(
    food
    .filter(c.meal_name.is_in(["Breakfast", "Lunch", "Dinner", "Snack"]))
    .group_by(c.id, c.meal_name)
    .agg(
        grams = c.grams.sum(),
        kcal = c.kcal.sum()
    )
    .ggplot(aes(c.grams, c.kcal))
    .geom_point(aes(color=c.meal_name), alpha=0.2)
)
```

4. Take the code from the previous question and add `.scale_color_cmap_d()` to change
the color palette.

```{python}
(
    food
    .filter(c.meal_name.is_in(["Breakfast", "Lunch", "Dinner", "Snack"]))
    .group_by(c.id, c.meal_name)
    .agg(
        grams = c.grams.sum(),
        kcal = c.kcal.sum()
    )
    .ggplot(aes(c.grams, c.kcal))
    .geom_point(aes(color=c.meal_name), alpha=0.2)
    .scale_color_cmap_d()
)
```

5. Now pick the colors yourself. Replace `.scale_color_cmap_d()` with
`.scale_color_manual(values={...})`, giving a dictionary that maps each of the four
meals to a color of your choice.

```{python}
(
    food
    .filter(c.meal_name.is_in(["Breakfast", "Lunch", "Dinner", "Snack"]))
    .group_by(c.id, c.meal_name)
    .agg(
        grams = c.grams.sum(),
        kcal = c.kcal.sum()
    )
    .ggplot(aes(c.grams, c.kcal))
    .geom_point(aes(color=c.meal_name), alpha=0.2)
    .scale_color_manual(values={
        "Breakfast": "orange",
        "Lunch": "green",
        "Dinner": "navy",
        "Snack": "red"
    })
)
```

6. Draw a scatter plot of `kcal` against `grams` for the individual items, colored by
`food_source`, with `size=0.5`.

```{python}
(
    food
    .ggplot(aes(c.grams, c.kcal))
    .geom_point(aes(color=c.food_source), size=0.5)
)
```

`food_source` has 27 categories, and nobody can tell 27 colors apart. The legend takes
up most of the figure. Color works best with a small number of categories.

7. Scales can also change an axis. Draw a histogram of `kcal` for the individual items
with `bins=40`, and add `.scale_x_log10()`.

```{python}
(
    food
    .ggplot(aes(c.kcal))
    .geom_histogram(bins=40)
    .scale_x_log10()
)
```

The whole range from 1 to 5,000 calories now fits, and there are two humps: food at
around 100 to 200 calories, and coffee, condiments, and lettuce leaves below 10. Read
the warning, though: 23,132 rows were removed. The log of zero cannot be drawn, so every
zero-calorie item was dropped without any sign of it in the plot.

8. Take the code from the previous question and add `.filter(c.kcal > 0)` before the
plot.

```{python}
(
    food
    .filter(c.kcal > 0)
    .ggplot(aes(c.kcal))
    .geom_histogram(bins=40)
    .scale_x_log10()
)
```

The plot is the same, but now the rows are removed in your code, where a reader can see
it.

9. Compute the number of items and the mean `kcal` for each hour (`time`), sort by
`time`, and draw a line plot of the mean calories against the hour.

```{python}
(
    food
    .group_by(c.time)
    .agg(
        n = pl.len(),
        mean_kcal = c.kcal.mean()
    )
    .sort(c.time)
    .ggplot(aes(c.time, c.mean_kcal))
    .geom_line()
)
```

10. The y-axis in the previous plot starts near 90, which makes the changes look larger
than they are. Take the code from the previous question and add
`.scale_y_continuous(limits=(0, None))` to start the y-axis at zero.

```{python}
(
    food
    .group_by(c.time)
    .agg(
        n = pl.len(),
        mean_kcal = c.kcal.mean()
    )
    .sort(c.time)
    .ggplot(aes(c.time, c.mean_kcal))
    .geom_line()
    .scale_y_continuous(limits=(0, None))
)
```

The `None` leaves the top of the axis to be chosen automatically. Items eaten in the
evening carry more calories on average than items eaten in the early morning.

11. Take the code from the previous question, but draw points instead of a line, with
the size of each point given by `n`, and add `.scale_size_area()`.

```{python}
(
    food
    .group_by(c.time)
    .agg(
        n = pl.len(),
        mean_kcal = c.kcal.mean()
    )
    .sort(c.time)
    .ggplot(aes(c.time, c.mean_kcal))
    .geom_point(aes(size=c.n))
    .scale_y_continuous(limits=(0, None))
    .scale_size_area()
)
```

`scale_size_area` makes the area of each point proportional to `n`, with zero mapped to
a point of no size. The hours in the middle of the night have very few items.

12. Facets split one plot into panels. Go back to the plot from question 3, remove the
color, add a line of best fit with `geom_smooth(method="lm", se=False)`, and add
`.facet_wrap("meal_name")`.

```{python}
(
    food
    .filter(c.meal_name.is_in(["Breakfast", "Lunch", "Dinner", "Snack"]))
    .group_by(c.id, c.meal_name)
    .agg(
        grams = c.grams.sum(),
        kcal = c.kcal.sum()
    )
    .ggplot(aes(c.grams, c.kcal))
    .geom_point(alpha=0.1)
    .geom_smooth(method="lm", se=False)
    .facet_wrap("meal_name")
)
```

The line for breakfast is flatter than the others. Breakfast has a lot of coffee, milk,
and juice, so a gram of breakfast carries fewer calories than a gram of dinner.

13. `facet_grid` takes two variables, one for the rows and one for the columns. Take the
histogram from question 8, filter to the four main meals, and add
`.facet_grid("at_home", "meal_name")`.

```{python}
(
    food
    .filter(c.kcal > 0)
    .filter(c.meal_name.is_in(["Breakfast", "Lunch", "Dinner", "Snack"]))
    .ggplot(aes(c.kcal))
    .geom_histogram(bins=25)
    .scale_x_log10()
    .facet_grid("at_home", "meal_name")
)
```

All the panels share the same axes, so their heights can be compared. Breakfast, dinner,
and snacks are mostly eaten at home; lunch is close to an even split.

14. Take the plot from question 12 and add labels with `.labs()`: an `x` label, a `y`
label, a `title`, a `subtitle`, and a `caption` saying that the data come from What We
Eat in America.

```{python}
(
    food
    .filter(c.meal_name.is_in(["Breakfast", "Lunch", "Dinner", "Snack"]))
    .group_by(c.id, c.meal_name)
    .agg(
        grams = c.grams.sum(),
        kcal = c.kcal.sum()
    )
    .ggplot(aes(c.grams, c.kcal))
    .geom_point(alpha=0.1)
    .geom_smooth(method="lm", se=False)
    .facet_wrap("meal_name")
    .labs(
        x = "Grams of food at the meal",
        y = "Reported calories at the meal",
        title = "A gram of breakfast carries fewer calories",
        subtitle = "One point per person per meal",
        caption = "Source: What We Eat in America"
    )
)
```

15. Take the code from the previous question and add `.theme_minimal()`.

```{python}
(
    food
    .filter(c.meal_name.is_in(["Breakfast", "Lunch", "Dinner", "Snack"]))
    .group_by(c.id, c.meal_name)
    .agg(
        grams = c.grams.sum(),
        kcal = c.kcal.sum()
    )
    .ggplot(aes(c.grams, c.kcal))
    .geom_point(alpha=0.1)
    .geom_smooth(method="lm", se=False)
    .facet_wrap("meal_name")
    .labs(
        x = "Grams of food at the meal",
        y = "Reported calories at the meal",
        title = "A gram of breakfast carries fewer calories",
        subtitle = "One point per person per meal",
        caption = "Source: What We Eat in America"
    )
    .theme_minimal()
)
```

16. Last question, and it is a written one. Name the plot you would use to answer each
of these, and say why in a sentence: (a) how are people's daily calories distributed?
(b) do people eat more calories at some meals than at others?

**Answer**: (a) A histogram or a density plot, since the question is about the
distribution of one numeric variable. (b) A boxplot of calories for each meal, since it
compares a numeric variable across the levels of a categorical one.
